Register of Letters and further writings which on this day by order of the Esteemed and Honored Mister Carel Koenad, Chief Merchant and Governor, together with the Council, have been prepared in readiness for Batavia and are dispatched by the Company's ship "The House in the Forest" over Malabar to that destination, consigned and addressed to His High Excellency, the High and Noble, strict, greatly esteemed Mister Abraham Patras, Governor General, together with the Well-Esteemed, strict, greatly esteemed Gentlemen Councillors of the Netherlands Indies, namely:

Register No. 1: An original missive dated 31 December 1737, and enlarged from Persia on 31 December 1737 with an appendix of today's date, by and to as mentioned in the heading, properly addressed.

No. 2: An original secret missive dated 3 February, in all humility to the most esteemed His High Excellencies, by as stated, presented.

No. 3: A copy missive by one as aforesaid, dated 4 April of the past year, sent by the small ship Rithem.

No. 4: Under seal from Bassoura, received here by the ship "D'Anthonia," a packet by the ministers there, addressed to their High Excellencies at Batavia.

No. 5: An original sealed packet for their Reverences, the gentlemen Orphan Masters at Batavia.

No. 6: Three copies of outgoing patrimonial missive dated 18 May 1737 by the Esteemed and Honored Mister Carel Koenad and councillor here, from Persia on 31 December 1737, to the gentlemen superiors in the fatherland, sent by the ship "D'Anthonia" to Bassoura, to be forwarded from there overland via Aleppo to the fatherland. Two similar ones dated 6 July and 1 September 1737 by the residents in Bassoura to as just mentioned.

text_translated_detailed: From Persia, dated the 31st of December 1743. Resolution taken in Council at Gamron on Wednesday, the 10th of April 1737. Present, all [members]. The Council, having been convened by the Lord Governor together with the others, was first presented with a report from the fiscal Christoffel de Haan, whereby it was established that the inspection of the small ship Ritthem at its departure, in accordance with the orders, had been properly conducted in the presence of two express members from the Judicial Council, it being of the same tenor as was indicated below. Report made in all respect to the Esteemed Lord Carel Koenad, chief merchant and governor over the Company's important interests in the kingdom of Persia with the jurisdiction thereof. In accordance with the well-known highly esteemed order of our Lords Majores, and your Esteemed further oral instructions, we, the undersigned, as express commissioned members from the Judicial Council, have on this day, together with the fiscal of this directorate, Christoffel de Haan, proceeded to the board of the ship Ritthem, lying here at the roadstead ready to sail, in order to return to Malabar and Batavia, Esteemed Lord, and from Persia, dated the 31st of December 1737, having mustered the crew of the same according to custom, inspected it to the best of our ability, finding therein no private goods, and the keel 15 feet clean, with its bow 16¾ [feet] scarce, with its stern deep going, thus hoping we have performed our duty, so we remain with the required respect, [undersigned] your Esteemed's obedient, obedient, and obligated servants. [Was signed] P. G. Nauman and A. Vink. [In the middle] before me [signed] C. l dehaan. [In the margin] Gamron, the 6th of April, Year 1737. Just as his Esteemed, in the head mentioned, also let it be known, how on the 7th of this month, by exhibition of his private letters, J. o from Batavia received, first discovered and found, a receipt.

Dated from Persia 31 December 1737. The Council, upon the summons of the Lord administrator, having come together with the others and having taken their proper places, came before [us] for resumption the wool accounts received from Hirman with the documents relating thereto, when one first observed the difference, to our regret, against our previously held opinion, and what had already been reported via Rottum to their high Excellencies, the esteemed great respected ones, the high Indian government at Batavia, that insofar as we were then able to ascertain, the man of 6 pounds of that wool would not have come to more than 15 shillings per pound, and according to the invoice it had also been charged to us accordingly, whereas we now saw with regret that the same came to 17 and 1/15 white [currency], which at first caused no small astonishment. Thus the Messrs. Simon Clement, Emanuel Martijn, and Frans van Loon were commissioned, each having purchased a portion of that wool, to confront the received accounts with the letters received from the merchant Auwannees at successive times. Dated from Persia 31 December 1737. Report given and delivered with all respect to the esteemed Lord Carel Koenad, head merchant and administrator of this Persian direction and its jurisdiction, as well as to the Council. — Commanding Lord and esteemed Lords, according to your Excellencies' orders, to examine exactly and most carefully the wool accounts most recently received on the 16th of this month from Hirman of the year 1736/7, prepared and sent by the merchant Godje Auwannees, we, the undersigned, in observance thereof, in the presence of the aforesaid clerk of this Gamron secretariat, Joris Brand, have effected the same, and according to most careful examination and confrontations of the letters sent by him at different times, found them to accord. And upon comparison of the old accounts of the previous year's August, or those of the year 1736/7 against the same, found that the quantity of wool purchased at that time amounted to 69,897 pounds, and that of this year only 61,560 pounds, therefore this year 8,337 pounds less. On the other hand, the expenses that this present account bears, as well as those of the previous year, were found to have been given in gifts at that time only 2,525 rixdollars, and now 11,155 rixdollars and 10 stuivers, it appears that thus more was spent on the smaller quantity purchased this year than in the previous year.

text_translated_detailed:
Gentlemen. In dutiful obedience and in accordance with your Esteemed order, we, as expressly appointed for this purpose, have proceeded in the presence of the fiscal of this directorate, the Esteemed C.l de Haan, to the Company's spice warehouse, where by the under-merchant and warehouse master, the Esteemed William Master, we were shown 4 chests with nutmegs of the Rompen sort, which were found to be extraordinarily damaged and harmed by worms. Also for that reason, according to your Esteemed order dated the 10th of this month, we set to work, and in the presence of the appointed commissioners saw them garbled [processed/cleaned], and the pure [nutmeg] separated, and found it to consist of a quantity of deliverable and good 500 pounds net, undeliverable and damaged — 193½, material lost in garbling 2. — lost in processing 4. — thus altogether containing a total of 699½ pounds, with which we hope to have dutifully observed your Esteemed order and provided the required satisfaction. We sign ourselves with deep submission.

From Persia dated 31 December 1737. [was signed] Esteemed Commanding Gentleman and Esteemed Gentlemen, your Esteemed's entirely obedient and faithfully obligated servants [was signed] L.r C.s Preson, and H. k v.n Poot [in margin] before me [signed] C.s de Haan [in margin] 1737 Gamron, the 17th of April 1737.

text_translated_detailed: April 1737, with the 199½ pounds [modern equivalent: approximately 90 kg] noted there being undeliverable and absent according to the order in the account books written off, and after consideration of the small minority, the executors of this Commission have accepted the offer of today as sufficient, and after this, most recently at the last rain that occurred, some leakage in the powder magazine has been discovered by the Constable of this Office, Stephanus Lapperson, so by order of the Governor, after inspection by expressly appointed commissioners, the following report has been made thereof. Report made and delivered in all respect to the Honorable Mister Carel Roenad, chief merchant and governor of this Persian direction and its jurisdiction, together with the Council. Honorable Commanding Sir, and Honorable Gentlemen, the undersigned of this office, according to the Commission laid upon us from Persia under date 31 December 1737, and for the observance of your Honorable esteemed instructions; have proceeded to the powder magazine beneath the northwest point of this Lodge, or behind the spice warehouse, in order to go there to inspect and exactly examine where a serious leakage, recently discovered and made known in the last rainy period by the Constable of this Office, Stephanus Lapperson, was occurring, so after the said magazine was properly emptied and all the gunpowder removed from it, we went inside in order to examine it all around with candles, when we found the vault, where the cannon of the aforementioned northwest point stands, to be burst and cracked, and even above the door to have notably sagged, through which cracks one could clearly measure the water that had remained there, the aforementioned leakage having been caused and brought about thereby, and no other reasons for the cracks and sagging could be given, than that the same, according to our humble judgment, shall have been caused by the severe earthquakes that occurred in the past and this year, and to which the highest repairs are required,

text_translated_detailed: Honored Gentlemen, in dutiful compliance with your Honored orders we, the undersigned, as duly commissioned in the presence of the warehouse master DE Willem Meester, under the brought goods and merchant's ship D'Anthonia here in the warehouses received one package marked no. 44 and containing 80 pieces of common bleached salempuri, of which the outer covering or outer cloth was found to be completely rotten and damaged, subsequently upon opening of said package discovered that thereof 52 pieces were undeliverable and stained with rust, and 28 pieces good, which we in duty bound have judged proper to report to your Honored in timely fashion, in expectation that we have thereby satisfied your Honored's desired purpose, we subscribe ourselves with reverence (undersigned) Honored Governing Sir and Honored Gentlemen, your Honored's obedient and faithful servants (was signed) I. H. Roscher and C. V. Rhee (in margin) Gamron on the 10th of April 1737. To the Honored Mister Carel Koenad, chief merchant and governor of this directorate, together with the Council. Honored Governing Sir and Honored Gentlemen. Persia dated 31 December 1737. text_translated_detailed: [In margin] Recalculated and booked (signed) M. K. Leipzigh [lower] approves (signed) as follows. Specification of the aforementioned travel expenses, incurred by the Company's interpreter Elias Sahid, on the journey from the village of Spahaneck [Ispahan] to Abergoe [uncertain: possibly Abarguh], which comprises several days' travel from this city of Spahan [Isfahan], with the court of the present ruler of these lands, Nadir Shah, which he had to undertake in order to obtain confirmation of the Company's latest orders from that authority. Since the 23rd of September, he was therefore compelled to follow from that village through Persia, dated the 31st of December 1737 until the 13th of December 1736, following which in the late evening he returned with the confirmed mandates to the Company's lodge. Namely, rations or subsistence allowances for 21 days that the round trip lasted, for the provisions in the camp and the entire road for food, both for him as interpreter and for his son Jacob Sahid, who was assigned to him by the bookkeeper Mattheus van Leipzigh as interpreter due to his age, in case it should become necessary, to accompany the scribes and others, and that he as interpreter had to entertain the people of the beglerbeg [Turkish provincial governor] Muhammad Taki Khan and other local lords from time to time, in total, according to the account kept by him, was disbursed. m. s 276 – ƒ 117. 6. Local servants' monthly wages. Subsistence allowance on the general journey to 1 servant for 5/8 of the daily rate provided m. 1 5/10 ir r: „ 23. - „ 9. 15. 8 Fodder and expenses for horses. 21 days' fodder for two Company riding beasts given to the aforementioned interpreters and son for the journey, disbursed daily m:r 6 4/5 comes thereafter. m. 138 /¾ . -

On the 28th of April last, two male slaves, in the ownership belonging to Lieutenant Anthony Jansz van Bercheijk and the Bookkeeper Ammon Sporrong, from a malicious intention by night, with the help of a rope, climbed the walls of this fortress, and through such a detestable means found the way to flight, which villains after the passage of some time and after much effort and expense applied, were caught by the natives and delivered into the hands of Justice, subsequently being condemned by sentence on the 6th of this month to be put in irons and for the period of 5 years to work on Batavia at the common works without pay, so it is hereby made known by memorandum what was given to the Regent in Minau and others for the securing of those persons. text_translated_detailed: Your Honors' most faithful servant from Persia under date 31 December 1737 from Batavia found a boy named Salmath from Boeton, and since no writing or secretarial paper was found, by which it could appear that the same was ever a male slave of his, although the said Balck, being in living memory, declared to me and various other persons that he, Hamath, was previously indeed in slavery to his uncle, namely Blois, but was also subsequently set at liberty by last will, under this condition nevertheless, that the aforementioned Hameth, he Balck, should have served him until his years of majority or married state, so the supplicant turns to the consideration of Your Honors and Gentlemen, and requests at the same time with respect order how one should conduct oneself regarding this matter, so I remain herewith in that hope and sign myself further (was signed) A Vink, (in margin) Gamron on 5 June 1737. Thus the supplicant was licensed the aforementioned life-servant under his supervision and for the performance of his household services, with the same to be provided with proper food and clothing, to be able to keep until the first opportunity when that service from Persia under date 31 July 1737 can be to Batavia, for the disposition of the Honored Guardians, as one learns from that side that the deceased Cornelis Balck, to have been under their honorable guardianship, shall be sent back. text_translated_detailed: Merchant and [Governor] of Persia under date 31 July 1737, Governor of this direction together with the Council, Esteemed commanding Gentlemen and Esteemed Gentlemen, [I] give with deep respect to know Your Esteemed [persons], the superior in service of the Esteemed Company, dutiful Servant Jan Willem Nieper, how after the death of the ship's bookkeeper of the Company's ship here at the Roadstead, the "Vrouwe Huijs te Foreest," Willem Adriaan de Wit, by whom he together with the [superior] on the ship Anthonia, the described superior Arnoldus Maxturne, according to a Codicillary power of attorney passed at this Office, before the first sworn Clerk on the date 30 May 1737, were requested to [receive] full power of attorney of his remaining goods, by Your Esteemed [persons] has been licensed to accept that estate, and since in the aforementioned power of attorney it is stated that his inheritance, as it was found, would be sent to Batavia to the Constituent's General Empowered [Agent], the Esteemed Rynard Jan Wiltens, Notary Public there, to whom the further care was entrusted, yet thereby some goods were found which are subject to spoilage from Persia under date 31 December 1737, and which constitute the greatest interests of that estate, [and] must be converted to money, so has the supplicant turned to Your Esteemed [persons] and Esteemed Gentlemen with humble request, [asking] him to license the sale by public auction of such goods as clothing, knives, hatchets, [and] clinkers, which are subject to spoilage, all the more because the supplicant needs the money for the payment of burial expenses and the satisfaction of some outstanding debts. /undersigned/ doing which &tc / in margin / Gamron on 27 June 1737. Which being done by the assembled present members, for the reasons given and probable [reasons] thereof, he was empowered [and] approved, and since the superior Nieper since September of the past year has received no supply of spices for the medicinal shop

text_translated_detailed: Monday the 8 July A.D. 1737, all present except the under-Merchants Cornelis van Rhee and Jan Will Schultsz, the first through indisposition and the last in civil arrest. With the Return of the English Ship Richmond from the Euphrates, brought here yesterday in the falling of the evening, a small letter by the bassourase from Persia under date 31 December 1737 Servants, under date of 20 June to the Mister Governor and this council, in reply to our letters of 31 January, which had served to accompany 12 Packages, linen goods and the like, sent with the same small vessel to those places, [was] directed, so let his Esteemed [person] the assembled members convoke today for the purpose that before the departure of the vessel, the cargo, which now lay as completely in readiness, to under God's guidance with the first favorable wind to steer toward Bendir à Boucher, the necessary [matters] for the response might be arranged, when from the cited writing it came to appear well to satisfaction, how the aforementioned goods had been received there, and the greatest part of that already sold, but so pleasant was not the news concerning 8 pieces found short in one package of fine muslins, just as this was confirmed from the sent [documents] and here inserted. Finding of such Twelve Packages, diverse Linens as we undersigned by order of from Persia under date 31 December 1737 the Merchant and first resident of this Office Georgie Gutchi from the English ship named Richmond in the Warehouses received, inspected and weighed on the scale, to wit weighing Number 19 weighing as described and according to here obtained up to as according to invoice on the scale Gamron & here 4 Packages Chamcarijs large 42„ — 315„—„— 314„—75„—324„-„—322„-97„—322„-„—321 71„—323„-„— 3 23 d 4 packages Chamcanijs weighing lb. 1284 — 1280 3 _=o Chamcanijs

text_translated_detailed: interim Warehouse Master de Novo being questioned as to what he could contribute to the clarification of that gross abuse regarding his responsibility, so he gave the following answer in evidence: that at the time of that shipment, at which he was otherwise always present according to duty, he had just the invoice of the shipment in hand, due to the acute illness of the Honourable Cornelis Engelsen, and in the meantime, he had recommended to the commissioners the accurate weighing of those packages and had entrusted them with it, and therefore hoped not to be held culpable. Which matter was then again considered and reflected upon by the council, that neither the aforementioned Pieter Dantel, since the packages were received unweighed and properly delivered on board the aforementioned ship, could be rightly addressed regarding this or suspected without foundation, nor the rogue's trick by the Englishman, committed on the outward voyage, since that nation, until now in this waterway, has not been able to allow themselves to be entrusted with any consignment goods or warehouse servants of ours, indeed they themselves have not been able to let themselves be entrusted with chests of money for transport, and therefore after further consideration as to what in the cash account could have served, it was arrested that the aforementioned 8 pieces of shekels, instead of being brought to the account of profit and loss (as for the drawing up of this the Bassoura residency from the notes held in passing is divided), should be paid at selling prices, namely the aforementioned warehouse master (notwithstanding the reasons given) one half and by the commissioners the other half, amounting to 336 or 142 guilders 16 [modern equivalent: Dutch guilders], as follows: for Willem Meester, 168 or 71 guilders 8 [modern equivalent: Dutch guilders], for Frans van Loon, 84 or 35 guilders 14 [modern equivalent: Dutch guilders], for Martinus Boudron.

We certify and declare, just as they certify and declare by these presents, how they, before their departure from Batavia to here in the aforementioned vessel, both in the hold and elsewhere, made a thorough inspection to ascertain whether everything was well provided and whether the hold was also tight, to prevent any damage from leakage. At which time they found everything tight and in good condition. The great beams, the carlings, and the great mast from below were properly provided with new braces, and likewise the hatches with good caulking, so that no suspicion of any leakage could have been entertained. And the Company's representatives further declared that upon arrival here at the roadstead, and after they had broken open the cargo, they found everything still well stowed, except that they discovered some leakage on the starboard side, which they presumed must have arisen from the heavy working of the ship during several storms encountered on the voyage back to here, near Ceylon and in this Gulf. With this, the Company's representatives concluded their declaration, testifying that it contains the pure truth, giving as the reason for their knowledge that they had observed and witnessed everything in such manner. And they remain further ready to confirm this same declaration with an oath (should it be required). text_translated_detailed: Nicolaas Duijt, by virtue of Your Honors shown to the suppliant most esteemed resolution, summoned from Persia under date 31 September 1737 and admonished, to from the estate and for the account of the deceased ship's bookkeeper Willem Adriaan de Witt, whose administration the supplicant according to Codicillary, by Your Honors on the 3rd July last ratified disposition, is entrusted, for the benefit of the Company to must, to compensate and pay, the sum of m.s 4234½ or ƒ 1799- 12-8 1/3, which amount the supplicant through lack of sufficient Cash, not being able, is from aforesaid estate to be able to seize, but since under him still rest some unsold goods, consisting in a male slave, some worked gold and silver, together with a parcel of worn linen, which one and other the Testator willed and desired that after his death should not be alienated, but to Batavia to his attorney be sent back, so turns the supplicant himself to Your Honors with humble request, to with their high esteemed orders to be able to be strengthened, how in this subject he shall have to conduct himself (below) which being done after deliberation with unanimity decided to grant the supplicant's request and to qualify him from Persia under date 31 December 1737 to the sale of the goods, in order the Honorable Company to her guarantee to come. ship the House at Foreest, Isaac Willemsz, finds himself compelled to present to Your Honored Excellency with due respect, how he and his subordinate ship's officers, on yesterday, being the 25th of August, from Persia under date 31 December 1737, took careful inspection and visitation of the fore mast in the aforementioned vessel, and after the timber at different places was examined, various cracks on the aft side and particularly at the middle section of that mast, running the same diagonally into the wood, in some places as much as 6 to 7 inches deep and ¼ thereof broad, were observed, and although we do not attribute those cracks to an excessive carrying of sail, but only to an excessive heat and dryness, yet the highest necessity requires that that mast, before this vessel puts to sea, be remedied and repaired by the application of a new wale [reinforcing timber]. Therefore the supplicant turns to Your Honored Excellency with humble request to be provided with such a wale or plank of a length of 36 feet and 20 to 22 inches thick, by means of which he hopes to put the timber in such a condition that, barring severe accidents, which God forbid, he will be able to undertake the voyage with this vessel to Batavia with confidence.

Furthermore the supplicant requests through Your Honored Excellency's good favor to be able to obtain for ship's use ¼ hide of pompleer [type of material] (understood), which being done from Persia under date 3 December 1737

text_translated_detailed: Letter to Congo dated September 8, 1737, and by the bearer of his letter received yesterday, the Constable said he was sent to Congo with the usual compliments and honorific titles concerning Your Excellency's predicament and the request made regarding four or five ship's carpenters who understand caulking work, and who would be greatly needed at this time for Laaff [uncertain: possibly a location name], to perform the same work on one of His Majesty's ships there and to put it in good condition. I find myself in great difficulty, since, God willing it otherwise, it will be clear enough that in the recently passed hot season, due to particular and severe illnesses, the number of upper and lower officers, along with the common men, has been reduced through death, and of those who remain, many still lie in miserable weakness. Your Excellency will be pleased to note this as a clear truth, since also against the will of heaven no one is able to do anything other than to console himself. And since among the deceased persons there are also effectively the most capable officers and workmen, to my particular misfortune, there is now a complete impossibility to fulfill Your Excellency's request, as there is but one who understands anything of it, and the other cannot be trusted with work of importance. Your Excellency is pleased to cite in a friendly manner such a craftsman or craftsmen for only a few days, and therefore I have not been able to know rightly the required time, which has also frustrated me in the meantime, since the ship and short days please God to return from here to Batavia, to my highly esteemed superior lords. And for the third matter, Your Excellency shall, it is hoped, have sufficient proof from Persia dated the 31st [of the previous month] 1737 and experience of the high regard which the Company maintains toward His Majesty himself, which has been demonstrated and carried out in proven services with full ships. However, all of this mostly runs counter to the highly esteemed commands of my superior lords, since their precious ships, through uncommon severe and dangerous voyages, after having arrived at Batavia from Europe, are then only sent hereward, and with that a command is always received under penalty of life to return as soon as possible, and no one, whoever he may be, from the ship's board to other services than the necessity of the Company's business requires, may be permitted to go. In such a way Your Excellency, through his particular experience among all European and other nations, will hopefully also agree, and for those reasons also be pleased to feel that I have been pressed in this matter, since the ship is mostly ready to depart, and the sending of the two remaining men against the order as stated and also not satisfying Your Excellency's esteemed requisite, I have nevertheless, out of regard for the close connection from Persia dated the 31st of December 1737, which is now struck with this Crown and great, God willing, as clear as the sunlight for everyone to see, with Your Excellency as a sincere friend of the Esteemed Company and myself.

text_translated_detailed: &c: To the Esteemed Mister Carel Koenad, chief merchant and governor of this Persian directorate, together with the council, commanding gentlemen and esteemed Mister Fredrik Emanuel Stips, chief master in the service of the Esteemed Company, stationed here at the roadstead on the ship called "The House in the Forest," it is respectfully made known that the medicines provided in the month of July have been consumed, and at present with daily increase there are many sick, finding themselves in the greatest distress, wherefore most humbly requests to be favorably granted the following medicines: namely 6 measures of spirits, 8 spoonfuls of oils, 10 Matrical, 8 ounces of sweet, 12 stomach remedy, 8 Cinnamon from Persia, dated 3 December 1737. From 8 measures of oil, 4 sweet, 3 Juniper, 4 wormwood, 4 centaury, 4 mallow, 3 camomile flowers, 4 saffron, 8 sarsaparilla root, 2 rhubarb, liquorice, 2 turpentine, 2 gum aloes, 1 myrrh, mastich and galbanum, 8 Vitnel from Cyprus, 3 pounds, 49 potash, 3 double arcanum, 4 Pantifbr, 2 linseed and fennel, 2 senna leaves, 3 Certi erin, 1 oil of verdigris, 13 white honey, 1 oil of Armenia, 1 small jar of rosewater, 30 cobalt grains of plaster cloth, 2 large plucking of Chamcanijs, etc. In the Dutch Comptoir Gamron on the 14th of November 1737 (was signed: E. Stips). From Persia dated 31 December 1737, being about the last, from observation of the fact that patients are collapsing very suddenly everywhere, who cannot always be properly brought to the hospital but are restored by the master's careful attention on board through medicine as well, just as this request was granted, as also after consideration of the required provision of what is necessary for the repair of the iron and the planks for covering the ballast, because of the wall not

text_translated_detailed: From Persia dated 31 December 1737, being about the last, from observation of the fact that patients are collapsing very suddenly everywhere, who cannot always be properly brought to the hospital but are restored by the master's careful attention on board through medicine as well, just as this request was granted, as also after consideration of the required provision of what is necessary for the repair of the iron and the planks for covering the ballast, because of the wall not being damaged again in the future, likewise the inevitable provisions for the people, as not being able to be missed, were noted and for that reason also resolved, on the 18th of this month from the last and regarding the iron and Chinese planks, by ordinance dated today to be distributed, under hope and humble trust that this entire transaction with the gracious approbation of the most esteemed and high noble, strict and greatly respected high Indian government in due time may be crowned. Thus resolved and arrested in the Dutch Comptoir Gamron, on the day, month, and year aforesaid: (was signed) C. Koenad, W. Master, A. J. V. Bercheijk and S. Clement, ad Int. Secretary. From Persia dated 31 December 1737. Resolution taken in Council of Gamron on Saturday the 30th of November 1737 in the forenoon at 3 o'clock, all present except the Mister Nicolaas Duijt and Cornelis van Rhee, both dismissed. In this meeting, after prayer held by the governor, the accounts for the months of August and September were reviewed, together with the given Spanish specification of the order and extra expenses made, found as those of the month of August to amount in total to 1558 measures, 662 rixdollars and 3 stuivers, of which extraordinary expenses amounted to 155 measures, 65 rixdollars, 17 stuivers and 6 pennies, as appears more clearly below. Extraordinary expenses brought by the bearer of this, consisting of a lamb

text_translated_detailed: The ship "The House at Foreest," brought from Batavia, which according to instructions was obliged to weigh post for post, and thus we have also had it properly recorded. Furthermore, it was asked whether the errors found therein should be corrected in the old books or in the new books. This was taken into consideration, notwithstanding that the Basra and Isfahan closed account books have already arrived here, and since those there had no knowledge of the changes in the errors found in their books, consequently the corrections had not been made. Nevertheless, it was deemed best that both matters should be corrected in the old books, and the residents at the aforementioned places should be notified of this as soon as possible. text_translated_detailed: envoy of the aforementioned Miersa, on 27 January 1738. Your letter has been well delivered to me, and the matter contained therein regarding your request for the Dutch is clear. To this I say that the politeness and friendship which I have always shown them was done so that they would repay the same with similar conduct, whenever this would be required in service of this Crown. But now that I have come, they have behaved ungratefully and have not served the King's interests. But because I had to depart quickly, I have not been able to punish them as they deserved, to serve as an example to others, but have had to postpone the same. However, I shall make it known to His Majesty by request, so that they may be punished by that Prince and their house be made a ruin. I have given an order to the Shahbandar [port official] Mahmed and the Hamcalem Aga Rafsie, in order that they shall take from other merchants what Your Excellency shall order them to take, and to set ship's orders concerning this, for if I come to learn that they have acted contrary to these my commands, I shall send someone to take their heads. Moreover, he has orally instructed the envoy Hossein Ali to tell Miersa that when the Dutch are willing to offer 1000 tomans [modern equivalent: a Persian monetary unit], which the Company's white money makes, 1200 tomans, or 51000 [uncertain: possibly a currency conversion], then he could accept the ship, and would then again show them all friendship as before and let them enjoy their former freedoms. But if they are not able to come to a resolution on this, Your Excellency must let them and their ships and vessels go forth from Persia under date of 31 July 1737. And have nothing more to do with them. (was signed) David Sahid.

text_translated_detailed: From Persia under date 31 December 1738 Ceylon To the Noble and Esteemed Lord, Gustaaf Willem van Imhoff [normalized version: Gustaaf Willem van Imhoff], Ordinary Councillor of the Dutch Indies, likewise Governor and Director of the Company's important operations in that widely extended Island, together with the Council: Noble, Esteemed, Earnest, Mighty, Wise, Foresighted and most generous lord and lords. By a French ship, Mr. Beamond, now setting course over Porto Novo toward Bengal, having been instructed in his appointed service, regarding the government of Coromandel, your Noble Esteemed [Lord], we hereby offer you the copy of our humble, last [letter] of 4 April of this year, and so we make use of the extraordinary freedom thereby to add the extract of the Proclamation dated 30 September of the preceding year sent forth, requesting an augmentation of 100 Balan [modern equivalent: a unit of weight] or 8000 pounds of fine Cinnamon; and for whose speedy fulfillment, we very friendly request of your Well-Esteemed [Lord] that his honored order may be given in such manner to obtain it, according to the remarks placed thereby, and for which we shall remain very obliged. — Meanwhile, we have not failed on the 27th of April of this year to request from the Persian residents everything that was required by your Well-Esteemed [Lord's] reverend request of 24 August, in the manner passed, Excepting the 4 cases of dragon vinegar, 100 pounds of radix liquoris, 10 [pounds] of marmalade, and for which in place for the departure of our own ship's opportunity we shall be able to obtain, to provide your Well-Esteemed [Lord] with the Uitspahan, being expected with the assortments, and already well packed in the warehouses lying 20,000 pounds of good ruinas roots [uncertain: possibly a type of root or plant material] to be arranged then. subordinate notice that the said quantity of radix comes to ƒ 11,333:6:8 [modern equivalent: Dutch guilders, shillings, and pence] r.m. text_translated_detailed: 1737 have been well brought to us together with the enclosed for Gamron, in original and duplicate, which packets respectively stand to be forwarded per first opportunity towards there, and as for what from us in the previous year; under humble request of address to Batavia, sent to your Esteemed Excellency, we have this with much respect to report, that therein we have indeed erred; but also at the same time no communicative matters for Cochin, or affairs concerning the General were concealed, and consisted only in disputes between Gamron and this Comptoir [modern equivalent: trading post] that resulted, dissensions, Over which we by those meager writings the rightful decision from their High Excellencies, the High Indian Government to Batavia, came to implore; Wherefore we most respectfully request your Esteemed Excellency to be pleased to interpret favorably for us that said papers were not dispatched under our flying seal, under promise however that in case we again over that route have something to dispatch to their High Excellencies or other ministers of the Esteemed Company from Persia, under date 31st December 1737, whereby the general, or anyone in particular comes to participate in some interest, we shall not fail to distribute the copies thereof ourselves where they might be judged to be of any use. In hope then Esteemed Excellencies, Earnest, manly, wise, foreseeing, and most generous Lord and Esteemed gentlemen, that your Esteemed Excellencies' displeasure through this granted satisfaction shall be ceased, we shall after a heartfelt wish of heaven's mild blessing over your Noble Excellencies' highly esteemed persons and precious interests of the Esteemed Company with singular respect take the honor to name ourselves (undersigned) your Esteemed Excellencies' submissive and obedient servants (lower) Agrees. (was signed) A. van Suchtelen (in margin) Basra this 20th June 1737 (undersigned) Agrees (was signed) J. C. Visscher sworn Clerk. To as before. Whereas

text_translated_detailed: and Pieter Auwagen, master carpenter, along with "ter Vlugd," had to be surrendered to the French, but in return we have again received from that nation on the Company's account a number of 7 deserters by name: Eve Noe, Thomas, Joan, Renier, Ghil, Crilard, Michiel, Gobbin, Pierre de Nouan, Louis Pillon. From Persia under date 31st December 1737, and Claude Utt. These boys, after some time had passed, requested assistance from us, since they were blood relatives of those who had fled from their vessel, and consequently needed something to provide them with clothing and such. This being considered in such a manner, we had each of them given 50 rixdollars [modern equivalent: Dutch currency] from the account of the forthcoming salary. However, Eve Noe and Michiel Gobbin, having come to buy at the shore and near the French settlement, were forcibly seized and locked in iron chains, from which two of them, however, the first one managed to break loose and escape his captivity, returned to our residence with the irons still on his legs. But the latter were sent to their ship. After this, the French employed all manner of tricks not only to gain their own men but also more of ours into their power, just as they had seduced them through promises from Persia under date 31st December 1737 of pardon for theirs and good treatment for ours. Thomas, Jean, Renier, and Ghil Crilard, along with the aforementioned carpenter Pieter Auwagen, so that at present we have retained only 3 pieces from that group, namely Eve Noe, Pier de Nouan, and Claude Ult., and in return we have lost the aforementioned three from ours, besides yet another much greater scoundrel, named Louis de Pillon, who is further recounted on day No. 28, dated 13th August.

Esteemed, pious, discreet ones, after the departure of our last letter, of which a copy, together with its register and the promised extract of Resolutions, goes herewith, we have received no advice from you, which greatly astonishes us and at the same time places us in difficulty regarding the obtained decree over 7 benjans [uncertain: possibly a measure or administrative division], concerning the deliberation of head-tax and such to be paid, since its non-existence prevents us from being able to reason with his Excellency Mhamed takkieChan on that subject with foundation. text_translated_detailed: Mister Dirk van Cloon (L.M.) has been made known and we have been promised further notification thereof; so you are now informed that according to the high command of which her High Noble, greatly esteemed Excellencies, dated 5th December in the year just passed, and the qualification obtained thereby for the public presentation of the most highly esteemed his Excellency, the High Esteemed, strict, greatly esteemed Mister Abraham Patras after the arrangement here from the 10th of this month, 5 days thereafter, with the required solemnities and ceremonies has been executed, and therefore you are hereby provided with a copy of the act of authorization and the formula of the oath standing thereto, after which everyone here has sworn loyalty to his present High Excellency Abraham Patras as Governor-General and lawful supreme commander in service, as you shall see from Persia under date 31st December 1737: the copy of the resolution taken on the last mentioned day regarding that important ceremony, as well as from the further attachments pertaining thereto, under recommendation to read all these writings with attention together, and the said presentation according to custom there, and the order brought with it dutifully executed, you must also let us know by a signed act, the proof that everything has been completed in conformity with the high order. Since it has been the gracious pleasure of the most esteemed her Excellencies to favor the bookkeeper Mattheus van Leijpzigh with the qualification of under-merchant and 40 guilders per month, under a new contract of 3 years, in conformity with the attached act; so we are in confidence, with the offering of felicitation that the same in this high favor, through all candor, zeal, and diligence, in his entrusted post shall endeavor to acknowledge, and answer according to all ability, and also the good expectation that one may have of him, so that he may profit even more in the future,

But concerning the unheard-of boldness of the copper [merchant] Hassan Poelet against the bookkeeper and second-in-command, with him having not only received a slap but even been thrown to the ground, and thereby injured his left hand, besides still other displayed unwillingness that a servant [uncertain: Tjattier] can show neither on a journey nor elsewhere, since now this boy has not yet returned to us, and it appears that through ignorance he has not earned wages according to his merits, since such a vice must not leave a nail on one of the toes through beatings and must be kicked out of service, we shall inquire further into this matter, and upon finding it, in the case that he should be caught at our cost, he must be punished as an example to others. We wish subsequently to trust that in the short term we shall soon receive notice of the happy arrival of our friends and caravan leaders. Persia dated the 31st of December 1737. Since on the 21st of this month a well-repaired and properly equipped vessel with merchandise has been arrested as a test under the good supervision of the second-in-command fiscal D.E. Jacob van Schoonderwoert, appointed as the foundation layer for the forthcoming progress in trade, to be sent to Bender à Boucher [Bandar Abbas] within approximately 8 days from now, amounting to approximately ƒ10,000 to ƒ11,000, we presume that upon the entry of the Southwest monsoon, the outward journey will be completed well by the end of July.

text_translated_detailed: Van Psia under date 31st August 1737, some trading goods as proof have happily arrived in a good condition; having been received very well and civilly by the present regents according to the country's custom, likewise having been flattered with a good prospect of the negotiation to be conducted, which however until now has been of very meager success, being somewhat attributable to the fact that the merchants from outside at Chiraas [Shiraz] as elsewhere, still have no knowledge of this undertaking, it being to be wished that when the same shall have become common knowledge, the merchants' courage will awaken and be encouraged to come to conduct a profitable and nearby located commodity trade, which success then will still have to be awaited with patience for some time, but it would be a desired matter for the Esteemed Company that here a vigorous merchant were found, with regard to the valuable returns that fall here from old copperware, weights, wheat-gold ducats, from Moors as otherwise, which all here are to be obtained for a civil price than elsewhere, and whereby then also the heavy otherwise calculated money loss here could be won out. God grant it success thereof. Van Persia under date 31st December 1737, on yesterday per express from the head Comptoir [Comptoir/office] with a missive of 5th August, sent to your Honour's residence, had resolved from her Honour's previously mentioned order, to send the goods at Cost [at the Company's expense] purchased by you and obtained goods over this route per Coffilah [caravan], for the alleviation somewhat of the heavy freight charges, for which reasons I then also will not hold the vehicle longer, but will send the same shortly Gamronwards [toward Gamron/Bandar Abbas], with some few obtained products of old copperware and wheat. text_translated_detailed: Esteemed, wise, prudent, discreet, and most generous Lord. Your Excellency, commanding Lord of Cassia, dated the 31st of August 1745. text_translated_detailed: daily report we leave from Van Persia under date 31 December 1737. We shall likewise relate this, to show Your Excellency what has been heard here since the 14th of April in the way of news and rumors, of which we shall briefly mention only that Nadir Shah, triumphing over his enemy Hassan Khan of Kandahar, would have closely confined him that same night in his fortress, so that that place would be in such a condition as Isfahan has had to suffer from that nation. Meanwhile, the victor, also having his eye on the Hendoustani [Hindustan], would gladly pluck some of his golden feathers from there. According to what is said, he has sent the former Albashik [Albashik: a high Ottoman official] to Kerman, the lord Mirza Reza, overland in an embassy, certainly for no other purpose than to seek pretexts so that, when no answer comes to his own unreasonable desires, he might fall upon the lands of the Great Mogul and from there, if possible, make a good haul. This, which then remains to be seen in due time, now seems finally to be earnest, that the Turkish ambassador, of whom much has been spoken, will arrive here in a few days. For the governor Hattembeecq [Hattembeecq] is busily engaged in preparing houses for him and his suite, which is said to consist of 3000 persons. And Nadir Shah's envoy, the Lord Abdul Baggie Khan, also finding himself in that company, is to be lodged, and all the properties are to be made ready with carpets. And the provisions given to that Turk, besides the firewood, of which 2000 men are needed daily, amounts to m:s 4000 or ƒ 1700.— per day. This certainly does not sit well in the purse of Wali Mahmed [Wali Mahmed], and now with the arrival of the ambassadors something will surely leak out, for the leading Ottoman Porte [Ottoman court] may well have something against this great man up its sleeve, which, when heard by us, shall be reported to Your Excellency in all fidelity, as we now do concerning the fate of King Thamas [Tahmasp II]. Since he still lives in his exile at Sabswaar [Sabswaar], the Persian treasurer, or Chazounadaar [Chazounadaar: treasurer], Mirza Bal Hassan, received an order a few days ago from Wali Mahmed to conduct the aforementioned women from the harem of that unfortunate prince, still here, with all honorable reception and suite of their servants and attendants, making the journey throughout the entire road from Corag [Qom] to that Van Persia under date 31 December 1737 Monarch, and to bring to His Majesty as a present and to cover the expenses 12 pieces of heavy mantles, 6 cargesses [uncertain: possibly a type of garment] or middle bands, some rich fabrics and other necessities, besides 5000 [uncertain: unit of currency] in cash, which was then again presumed to be a deceptive game on the part of the sender. But God alone knows what will come of it. In any case, the women are making their preparations to depart from here in a few days, and may Almighty God grant that the chances turn to the advantage of that lamentable worthy King to everyone's astonishment.

text_translated_detailed: Highly Esteemed Ambassador, we offer a copy of these matters with this letter in all respect, and we shall conduct ourselves for the most part in accordance with the contents thereof in the utmost humility, and make only a brief reference to it in this letter. That letter was principally directed at maintaining a correspondence of letter exchange. Furthermore, therein praising the wisdom and greatness of soul of the much-esteemed Persian ambassador, the Mister Abdul Paggie Chan, regarding his Excellency's conduct at the Turkish court, in the fortunate conclusion of the matter from Persia under date of 31 December 1737, bringing about the settlement of the differences between these two Muslim peoples, over which all the Turkish ministers were very content, as they pressed together to express their satisfaction to him. Among other things, they recommended to us that we maintain a residence with the gentleman and, in due course, also with the Turkish minister, such that one of the Persians here at this Persian court in Constantinople shall do likewise, for the facilitation of commerce and the exchange of letters and knowledge. With the wish, among other things, that likewise a peace between the Turk and the Russian court might be concluded for the general welfare of all Christendom, to which the King of England and their High Mightinesses the States General of the United Netherlands applied themselves greatly, in order if possible to bring the course of that War to a close. Accordingly, his Imperial Majesty, likewise with greater zeal working toward this, had his mediation offered at the Porte for that purpose, so that he might see himself freed through the conclusion of some peace from his engagement with the Muscovite, his ally. Meanwhile, the Mister Baron the Talman, Ambassador of the last-mentioned Majesty, was requested by the Grand Vizier, who was to winter with the army at the banks of the Danube, in the encampment of the Ottomans.

Since I am certain that the Mister hadje Mhamed Costijsch, shahbandar [port official] or toll-master, first departed from here on the 16th of September on his journey there, with the letter which I, together with the second [copy] of this Office, Monsieur Joris Brand, shall have had the honor, on the 4th of this same month, per the 5th in all humility to present to your Esteemed Honor, your Esteemed Honor will have appeared long before the arrival of this letter, therefore a copy is sent herewith, you are excused, but I take the liberty to have this presented to Your Esteemed Honor for your consideration, of the copies and translations of the two Persian letters, which were sent through the said toll-master to his Highness the Beglerbegi [Ottoman provincial governor] Mhamed tackie Chan, and his second Aga Jaffer, and by ours were promised to send the same to Your Esteemed Honor by a later occasion, which, as said, is now first happening, so I request Your Esteemed Honor most humbly to conduct yourself well toward me in this matter. From Persia under date 31 December 1737, as well as toward the aforementioned letter most respectfully. Since then I have had the great honor to receive Your Esteemed Honor's always much respected letters dated the 13th of December and the 7th of September last, together with the enclosures attached thereto, per the private merchant's runner by the name Sjaboen and hadje allie

text_translated_detailed: as said, which is now first happening, so I request Your Esteemed Honor most humbly to conduct yourself well toward me in this matter. From Persia under date 31 December 1737, as well as toward the aforementioned letter most respectfully. Since then I have had the great honor to receive Your Esteemed Honor's always much respected letters dated the 13th of December and the 7th of September last, together with the enclosures attached thereto, per the private merchant's runner by the name Sjaboen and hadje allie on the 5th of September and the 10th current with particular affection, upon which now, according to due obligation and duty, serving in reply in all respectfulness, I shall say that it was very agreeable to me to learn that our letter per the Company's runner Hossein pollat and the private one mentioned just above, ditto Sjaboen, directed to Your Esteemed Honor, had met with the good fortune of a successful delivery, and that Your Esteemed Honor had given the said pollat, for his presumptuous behavior and conduct toward the two gentlemen Branden Crane, wages according to his deserts, etc. In the meantime, Your Esteemed Honor had also seen fit to approve as well done, we, according to custom, having received the known last exchange letters reimbursed according to the first of the same, had delivered them to their holders. From Persia under date 31 December 1737, 7 of his proxy kewelraam Teddani, of which by the appendix of the 6th of August Your Esteemed Honor was most respectfully informed, good news has been received that the seed was sent per the runner Rostam, but the porter thereof has not yet appeared, though the same is expected at all moments, if nothing unfortunate has befallen him through the plague sickness in the upper lands, or other unexpected misfortunes

text_translated_detailed: From Persia under date 31 December 1737, 7 of his proxy kewelraam Teddani, of which by the appendix of the 6th of August Your Esteemed Honor was most respectfully informed, good news has been received that the seed was sent per the runner Rostam, but the porter thereof has not yet appeared, though the same is expected at all moments, if nothing unfortunate has befallen him through the plague sickness in the upper lands, or other unexpected misfortunes has happened to him, for which reason I am compelled to wait for him a few more days, and should he still not appear, I shall have it inquired after there through the said benJaar. text_translated_detailed: From Persia, dated 31 December 173[7], Ispahan [Isfahan], To the Esteemed Mattheus van Leipzig [van Leijpzigh]: Under Merchant and Head, together with the toll [official] Elias Sahie, concerning the Company's affairs there. text_translated_detailed: The highly esteemed order of the Honorable Mister Carel Hoenad, chief merchant and governor of the Persian directorate, together with the Council at Gamron, contained in their highly valued accompanying letters dated the 7th of May last, or at our departure from the aforementioned head office toward Costia [Bandar Abbas], to the fulfillment of which the undersigned would have proceeded according to duty much earlier, had he not been frustrated therein by the report of the accompanying merchants that they were not aware of the route over Feod to Costia, as it being our salt passage through that place, and also not until today had the same become known to them; for which reasons the undersigned then hopes that not only this taken delay, as having been done out of necessity, will be regarded by Your Excellency with a favorable eye, but also that the aforementioned esteemed missive with its accompanying attachments shall remain in your possession, since the same is still needed and principally concerning the freedom from toll and customs duties up to 20,000 thalers [modern equivalent: Persian currency], in order to show to the customs collectors on the way, so that thereby a freer passage for the Company's Caravan from Persia, dated the 31st of December 1737, might be obtained. Since the aforementioned departure until today, such matters of business have occurred as the undersigned upon his arrival at Costia (God willing) will have the honor to report to Your Excellency in a brief daily account, since due to the shortness of time and because we are now so near or today tomorrow and the village of Warzend, which is still four days' journey according to the report of the toll collectors from Spahan, has been reached, none of the matters herein shall be cited, under the hope of a gracious explanation, with which, Esteemed, pious one, and the Company's weighty concerns at Costia, commended to the protection of God, I remain with respectful greeting and

text_translated_detailed: From Persia dated the 31st of December 1737. Bandar-e Bushehr. To the Honorable Jacob van Schoonderwoert, Bookkeeper and provisional Fiscal, as well as Commissioner in the Company's affairs there. Esteemed, pious, discreet one. From Your Excellency's sent letter of the 24th of August of last year, by the hired courier Nasir, we learned yesterday with particular joy of Your Excellency's safe arrival with the vessel, crew, and goods at Costia; six days before the departure of the aforementioned advice, our rejoicing would have increased even more had we not seen in that report that Your Excellency's lengthy journey had still been accompanied by calms and considerable heat, since one of these had caused us to obtain some water and wood here and there, for an amount of 73 rixdollars [modern equivalent: Dutch East India Company currency], and in which one must console oneself. Concerning Your Excellency's meeting and treatment with the regents who were present at their arrival, we can see nothing other than that the same was well done according to local custom and also seems to include good consequences, both regarding the merchants' shown desire and eagerness for trade, as well as concerning the prices of old copper, Persian goods, grain prices and wheat, and trusting that Your Excellency will see to it that further reports of our heartfelt wish to the gentlemen masters in interest and glory shall be fulfilled through Your Excellency's conduct, which God grant. In the meantime we also approve Your Excellency's actions undertaken. From Persia dated the 31st of December 1737. And the expenses paid at the house that the Naib named Mhamed Resa has had cleared for Your Excellency, we will not doubt that the masters' left recommendation will serve Your Excellency very well with the further regents upon return, being furthermore the retention of the Indian letters for the Gentlemen Hassan Ali Baecq and Mhamet Prafie, in order to

text_translated_detailed: we also approve of Your Excellency's actions and accept the report from Persia dated 31 December 1737. — and the expenses incurred at the house that the naib [governor] named Muhammad Reza has had arranged for Your Excellency, in which we do not wish to doubt that the master's departed recommendation will serve Your Excellency very well with the further regents upon return, and we further consider the retention of the enclosed letters for the gentlemen Hassan Ali Baig and Muhammad Pasha well done for the reasons given, since through personal delivery Your Excellency will also be able to send them more securely. For the rest, we shall continue to oversee the already begun work of the accurate measurement of the situation and location at the coast through the pilot chief steersman Jan Martensz, in person as much as possible, together with Your Excellency's advice and specifications, since the good monsoon toward Batavia is at hand and it is to be hoped that the Anthonia, which small ship God willing, having spent two months on the journey to Basra, will also make haste to return to Your Excellency and to us, so that we may then present a perfect report of this administration to their High Excellencies in all obedient respect. We are meanwhile satisfied with the dispatch of our letters to the said Residency on 21 August as mentioned, and likewise with Your Excellency's intention to map out Ispahan regarding its appearance and condition at the coast, not doubting that those servants will make known to us the receipt thereof in due time, with which we conclude and remain, having referred to our accompanying attachments below, with respectful greetings, Esteemed, Pious, Discreet [undersigned]: From Persia dated 31 December 1737. Your Excellency's good friend [was signed]: C[olonel] Koenad, W[illem] master A[braham] S[imon] van Bergheijk, N[icolaus] Duijt, J[ohannes] H[enrik] Roscher and J[acques] Clement; [in margin]: Gamron, 13 September 1737, the bearer of this is mentioned.

Regarding what has transpired with the Regents since my previous last letter of 24 August, it should be noted that on the 2nd of September we were honored with a complimentary welcoming letter from the Naib [administrator] of the Landscape, at that time the Mister Hassan Ali Pasha, which I reciprocated the following day with a counter-compliment, the translations of which are now enclosed herewith. Furthermore, upon the return of Seyid Masqur, I could not refrain from presenting a gift for the cultivation and maintenance of true friendship to him and the Shabandhar [harbor master] Hadji Ali, whose friendship in this place is of great importance, the value of the gift being as shown in the attached list, amounting to a purchase price of ƒ49:6:—, hoping that the same may be approved and graciously accepted by Your Excellencies; as likewise another inevitable gift given on the 14th of this month to the Sardar Mirza Meg, the son of the Beglerbeg [provincial governor] Mamet Taki Khan, amounting to a purchase price of ƒ175:19:—, and of which the ship Persia under date of 31 December 1737 has provided official confirmation. This young man has strengthened here a great burden for everyone and makes requests daily now for this and then for that, such that I have even been forced to hand over my two only chairs to him, and for which reason I now find myself in great difficulty. And therefore, on the 27th of August last, not wishing to cause any offense regarding the friendship, I found myself obliged to accept as a gift a horse from the aforementioned Seyid Masqur, which also necessarily required a counter-gift in return, which I however only valued at the worth of one-eighth of an animal, amounting to a purchase price of ƒ101:3:—. The same is a grey-colored Taboo [horse breed], eight years old, valued by various merchants at 530 maunds.

text_translated_detailed: December 1737. On the way from Gamron to Spahan, A.D. 1737, June, audience was granted by that gentleman, where I was received very courteously and was treated in his Persian manner. There was shown for the further matter the aforementioned ferman with the confirmation of the Beglerbejle [provincial governor] Mahmed Tackie Chan. After this, that gentleman said to me: if you should need anything, please make it known to me without hesitation, I shall be helpful to you in all things and shall be. His Majesty has also ordered me to show all help and assistance to the Hollanders whenever they might need the same. To which I replied to that gentleman that beyond the difficulty of lack of beasts in which we had been and which we had now already been relieved of through the help of that Rais [captain], I had not needed anything other than his favor and assistance regarding the Company's affairs. To which that gentleman replied that he would in all circumstances show signs of his true affection and willingness toward the Esteemed Company, and that he would therefore, to ease me somewhat on the way and to show his goodwill, order his secretaries to have a tallega [travel permit] prepared for the Rahdaars [toll collectors] under his jurisdiction, so that we would not always be compelled to show them the King's fermans [royal decrees]. For all of which that gentleman I thanked, and he further inquired after the health of His Highness the Beglerbejle and His Esteemed the Lord Governor. To which this gentleman replied as much as I was aware of from the 14th of Persia under date 31 December 1737, A.D. 1737, June. On the way from Gamron to Spahan, and everything was satisfied, and I obtained shortly thereafter my leave and returned again. The promised tallega being delivered, together with a gift consisting of a dish with 10 [items], a [vessel] with fruits and flowers.

text_translated_detailed: the village of Naadonsjan, the 19th, the 20th, the 21st. Persia under date 31 December 1737. From A.D. 1737, June. On the way from Gamron to Spahan, where the holder of this [document] showed to a Rakdaar of Tesd called Hassan again the regam of His Majesty with the old tallega of the Wakiel to Tesd; and thus obtained a freer pass, offering to that boy, because he showed himself very serviceable, a little spices, pepper, and candy sugar, and there was also delivered the obtained tallega of Tesd after first having taken a copy of it. Wednesday nothing happened except that the Ioaloadhars still remained here. Thursday night around 2 o'clock we set out on our way, and had a steady good road. We arrived thus around 8 o'clock at a dilapidated house, or the manril Grumha Hoen, as the Toulodhaers were pleased to name it. We had reasonably brackish water here, which, to show its quality even more, had to be drawn from some stone cliff caves that on the sides were sown with a good quantity of so-called saltpeter. Friday morning around 4 o'clock we continued on our way, which was reasonably good, and arrived around 7 o'clock at a Caravanserai, the first that we encountered on the way, being around 20 feet high, built of heavy clay. Further around 50 to 60 feet high with baked brick and lime, built by order of the Persian King Abbas the Second in the year after the flight of Mahomet, the year 1610, so that from a structure of arduous stone hewn out, there was a carved inscription to be read, A.D. 1737, June. From Persia under date 31 December 1737. On the way from Gamron to Spahan, having this structure, as our report was, had as its cause the discovery of an underground water course through a canal, for when the aforementioned monarch.

text_translated_detailed: Stone and Lime built by order of the Persian King Abbas the Second in the year after the flight of Mohammed, the year 1610, as is evident from an inscription carved in hard stone, dated in the year 1737 June. From Persia under date 31 December 1737. On the road from Gamron to Isfahan, having [this building], our report was informed that the construction had as its cause the discovery of an underground water source through a deer, for when the aforementioned monarch had arrived here at a certain time with his army and the lack and uncertainty of finding it had been made known to him by his general, he thereupon gave orders to release one of the deer which had been taken along at that time and to set it loose and to follow carefully and pay close attention to the place where that deer might come to drink, which having been done, this water source was thereby discovered, and thereupon by order of his Majesty, in memory of this remarkable occurrence, this caravanserai was built and is called the gazelle or deer water; the same is somewhat brackish but still suitable enough to drink. Saturday the 22nd of this month in the afternoon around 5 o'clock we set out on our journey again and arrived the next morning around 4 o'clock at a small village provided with provisions but muddy water; we took our rest there. This place is called a way-station. Sunday night around 12 o'clock we set out on our journey and arrived the next morning around 8 or 9 o'clock in the village of Warsena, where the holder of this [document] received orders from the Honourable Mister Carel Koenad, chief merchant and governor of this Persian directorate, together with the Council at Gamron to deliver [the letter] and the letter was ready. 23rd of this month, 26th of this month. From Persia under date 31 December 1737, year 1737 June. On the road from Gamron to Isfahan.

text_translated_detailed: Persia dated 31 December 1737 A perfect description of the situation of Bandar Abbas [Bander à Boucher] with its harbor, banks and shallows that lie in the sea and before the inlet thereabouts, as well as how the surrounding places and the Castle Nadria are situated, and likewise a Compass and we placed it there at point A. according to the indication of the plan, we took bearings and found that the angle CAB was 117 degrees 30 minutes, the angle DAB was 96 degrees, the angle EAB was 72 degrees, the angle FAB was 50 degrees 30 minutes, the angle GAB was 23 degrees, the angle HAB was 12 degrees 30 minutes, taking then my course straight south 500 Rhineland rods [modern equivalent: approximately 1,750 meters] as to point B, I took bearings there and found the angle ABC was 48 degrees 30 minutes, the angle ABD was 64 degrees 30 minutes, the angle ABE was 178 degrees 30 minutes, the angle ABF was 94 degrees 30 minutes, the angle ABG was 129 degrees 45 minutes, the angle ABH was 149 degrees 15 minutes, seeing from here a thick tree to the southwest of my position, which could also serve as a fixed point for my purpose, I named it with the letter I, found the angle DBH was 110 degrees, taking from here my course again straight northwest-north at 260 rods [modern equivalent: approximately 910 meters] as to point K, I took bearings of the angle BKI at 45 degrees 30 minutes, seeing an old temple to the west-southwest of my position which I named with the letter Z, I observed the angle IKL and found it to be 52 degrees 30 minutes, going then to the old building L, and found there the angle KLI was 105

From Persia dated 31 December 1737. Specification of the following provisions, rations, allowances in money, and further necessities ordered by Commissioner Jacob van Schoonderwaart for the European seafaring personnel aboard the vessel the Bouche, provided since 18 August when it arrived here until this date when this vessel lies at anchor from this roadstead to proceed to Gamron [Bandar Abbas], costing as follows:

To Jan Martens, first mate, for 25 months cost money since 11 July when departing from Gamron until 11 December next, namely: 140 guilders. 230 pounds of rice for the same and 3 mats since 1186 [uncertain: possibly a date reference] until 11 December next at 2 guilders 8 shillings 6¾ per measure of schaers [uncertain: type of measure]: 95:— 120:—. Cadjang [uncertain: possibly a type of provision] at 3 mats, at 1 per man: 17½ 12. Can of vinegar at 1¼ per can: 15:—: 12 pounds of butter at 6 per man: 10½ 72 pieces of dried fish at 4 for 1 man: 18.— 12 pounds of tamarind at 4 per man: 7:— 60 man-portions of firewood of 1018 pounds at 2 per man: 120:—: 20. Of 6¼ meat at 1¾ per man: 35:—: for vegetables: —. 5 guilders for repairing and maintaining one large cooking kettle and installing a new bottom. Item, completely renewing one cooking pan: 13:— for tinning all the ship's goods: 67 guilders 4:— one water carrier for drinking water during the entire stay: 30. Comes to 87½ stuivers [modern equivalent: small Dutch coin] per man, reckoned for 510 men: 216:— 15 guilders. From the Company's stores: —:—: 18 12 pounds of powder, cost according to the books. Total: 217 guilders 13 shillings:—. Hendrick Aboucher, 20 September anno 1737, was signed. Jan Mertensz, [unclear title]. Agrees, was signed. V.K. Van Schoonderwaert, [unclear]. Agrees, was signed. Abraham van Juchtelen.

105. 44. 12. 8. From Persia under date 31 December 1737. Specification of the following rations for inland servants, monthly wages, necessary household expenses, travel and extraordinary expenses, item cash accounts, last [month] 7 November 1737, messenger wages, which since 11 July when departing from Gamron until the last of this month have been disbursed as follows:

Ration money for the first mate fiscal and Commissioner Jacob van Schoonderwaart since mid-July until the last of this month: 105 guilders. David Bufkens, assistant, likewise: 76 175.— 74 guilders 7 shillings 8 pence.

Inland servants' monthly wages: 1 servant for the Commissioner J. van Schoonderwaart since departure from Gamron until this date at 30 per month: 1 cook at 25 per month since as mentioned: 1 porter since arrival in Loed [uncertain: place name] at 25 per month: 35:—. 1 water carrier likewise 30 per month: 42. 1 farash [uncertain: possibly a sweeper or servant] or sweeper as above at 20:—: 28. 251:—. 106 guilders 13 shillings 8 pence.

Necessary household expenses for night light and firewood at 75 per month since 19 August when they came to reside here. For extraordinary expenses as much as since arrival beyond the ordinary rations through scarcity, dearness, and difficult procurement of provisions has been disbursed: 80 guilders. Inland scribe for writing a letter to the lord Hassan Ali Beg, likewise copying his Highness's fallega [uncertain: possibly a type of document] and paper: 15:—: paid. Further for the numerous visits of the gentlemen and merchants upon my arrival here, for coffee, rose water, tobacco, etc.: 27. To the bearer of a present from Chios, Maskoer [uncertain: place name], consisting of 3 sheep, 2 hens, and 2 bottles of rose water: 15:—: 187.— 58 guilders 4 shillings 8 pence. Carried forward: 668.— 283 guilders 18 shillings 4 pence:—:

Travel expenses. During the journey from Gamron to arrival at Loco [uncertain: possibly a place name] in 39 days with the vessel the Bouche, through uncommon heat, water was fetched seven times and firewood once at the passing places and villages, for whose speedy procurement in order not to delay the journey, to the helpers of the said vessel's crew, likewise also sometimes for some provisions, has been disbursed: 69 guilders. text_translated_detailed: Persia dated 31 December 1737. Accounting, as properly made with the Company's brokers, Ottoman [uncertain: possibly referring to Ottoman-related transactions], Cummertjent [uncertain: possibly a type of broker or agent] and Abtjent [uncertain: possibly a type of broker or agent]. Ledger page. Month. Hour. 1737. Until 14 November of that same year as Hour 6. Month. Part. Remainder of their previously remaining debt according to the Negotiation Books 547,327¼. 8 September 19. Sale to Merchants. Since 1 September. 88,623. 9 September 14. 169,866. The same. 19 September. 81,243. The same. The same. Received Cash from the loaned to Minouw [uncertain: possibly a person's name or title]. 1,482: 1/5 up to 600 thousand. (Remainder today still 51,104: 1/5). Sum of the brokers' debit. Rix-dollars 718,676. But placing. 718,676 off at 8½ stuivers [modern equivalent: Dutch currency subdivision] per rix-dollar. Reduced comes to ƒ [guilders] 305,437: 6. Following their Ledger favorable positions. Month 76. Page. Until 14 September. Over designated expenditure according to ordinances. Rix-dollars 40,134. November 14. Sale of their permitted brokerage at 1 percent. Comes to 169,866. Above mentioned. The same. The same. Cash or as much of the same therein in Cash in various species held in waiting for the expected Kirman [modern equivalent: Kirman, Persia] bills of exchange (as being for the New [uncertain: possibly referring to a new accounting period] until today not more paid than 230) and for the doing of the inevitable Lodging and ship Expenses as well as for the purchasing of old Copper from Merchants who do not want to Accept anything else for it, furthermore is thereunder also included the in stock being old Copper and thus together; 427,294. Comes. 469,127. By the brokers Spanish bills of exchange up to 249,549. Sum as above. Rix-dollars 718,676. Signed. This 14 November 1737. Undersigned. For the Cash and accounting. Was signed. Colonel Koenad, W. m Master. On the side stood. In Council the 5 December 1737. Shown to me and with pleasure condescended according to the instruction. Was signed. Abraham van Suchtelen. Persia dated.

text_translated_detailed: S. Conings, secretary of the trading post, who again took charge of the recognition of goods and the payment of tolls, etc., for conducting the Company's trade in these lands, was to set down in the matter as in its first inception to smother it upon the favorable approval of the Esteemed and Excellent Lord Carel Koenad, merchant and appointed governor of this Persian directorate, together with the respective council at Gamron [Bandar Abbas], promised and the agreements confirmed as desired, having obtained thereafter. First were given and presented, namely from the Company's stores the following, to wit: cinnamon for purchase and sale, 6 1/5 pounds, being so much as still remained as a remainder, presented to the first negam [official], in writing. The lord Mierse Megdie, who has much favor from the Nadir Shah and consequently great influence with the same, costing per pound in small pieces ƒ—: 10. 12, and the current selling price m. 120 or ƒ 51 per man [unit of weight] of 12 4 pounds, comes for the remainder or to make even in small pieces for purchase and net for selling price - ƒ - per Cassas [treasury]. Pomegranate juice for authenticating the agreements, presented to the Cadi [Islamic judge] or first ecclesiastical judge of this city Isfahan, in the name Miersa Rahiem, costing ƒ 8. 1. 10 3/15 per carat, net purchase, and against m. 35 or ƒ 14:17. 8, such that now the piece thereof was reckoned, comes in net selling 16. 3. 5 „ 29: 15. text_translated_detailed:
From Persia under date 31 October 1737. Memorandum of such goods as on the last day of July in the year 1737, by the residents of this Comptoir [Comptoir: trading post] in the name and on behalf of the Esteemed Company were presented to the now serving provisional broker Nagha Fattitjent and the Serraf [Serraf: money changer] or money changer Nagha Tettre to the honor of their positions, in order that in their valued services the Esteemed Company and we remain faithfully and with vigilance to continue serving, consisting and costing as follows, namely:

From the broker Nogha Sattitjent:
1 piece of sulband [sulband: turban cloth] worked through with gold, costing: 100:–
1 fine shawl for the body: 180
1 [shawl] for the shoulders: 110
1 zouratse allegia [zouratse allegia: striped fabric] with good stripes: 120
amounting for the broker in total: 510. ƒ216:15.

Serraf Negh Tettre:
To the [broker]:
1 piece of sulband with some gold worked through, no.: 80:–
1 shawl for the body: 110:–
1 [shawl] over the shoulders: 95
1 zouratse allegia: 90
amounting for the serraf in total: 375:. 159:7:8

These honor clothes amount together to: 885. ƒ376:2:8

In the Netherlands Comptoir Bassora [Bassora: Basra], this last July in the year 1737. (was signed) G: Gutchi and Abr. van Suchtelen (undersigned) agrees (was signed) Ab=m van Suchtelen (undersigned) agrees (signed) M. e vn dr Crap sworn Clerk.
